name: Victor Mensah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thank you for having me, Victor. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't tied to any company, union, party or government, and we don't sell anything. Everything you say is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Is that fine?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Yes, that's fine. Come in, mind the boots. Abena will bring tea in a minute, she wants to hear this too.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Abena and I bought Coldharbour Farm ten years ago, 140 hectares with a big mortgage from the bank. We keep 16,000 free-range laying hens in two sheds, and grow wheat and oilseed rape on the rest. I'm up at five to check the birds, the water and the feed lines, then the eggs are collected and packed with Stan and Jola, who work for us. Afternoons it's the fields, or mending something. The bird flu rules wear me out, every winter they keep the hens inside and the paperwork doubles.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Abena does the books and the egg sales, and our children are Kwame, who's twelve, and Grace, who's eight. Sundays we're at church, where I'm an elder. We've worked hard and saved, so there's well over six months put away and the farm's worth a good deal more than we owe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, now we can stop talking about it and get on with work. At church I'd say a hard day's work still counts for something. Online I'd stay quiet, it's not my place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it means the same worries as before, mainly bird flu and the egg contract. The packer renews our contract in 2027, and they always try to squeeze the price. One case of bird flu at Coldharbour Farm could cost me more than any computer ever will.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on as I am, with the same hens and the same people. I'd build up a separate reserve, maybe twenty thousand, just for a bird flu year. I'd use the AI now and then, like I do for letters to the packer, and that's all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little uneasy, but it's the old unease. Farmers always have something to worry about, and mine wears feathers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you use AI for letters to the packer. How did that start?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My neighbour Hugh showed me at a farm meeting how he used it for a complaint letter, and it was good. So I tried it for our egg contract. It writes more politely than I do when I'm angry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If bird flu hit, what would you do first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Phone the vet and the ministry, then sit down with Abena and the bank. We'd lose the flock and be empty for months. That's why the reserve matters, because the compensation never covers it all.

say: I'd say **good**, now let's stop talking and get on with work.
I'd say at church that a **hard day's work** still counts.
think: My real worries stay the same: **bird flu** and the egg contract.
The packer renews in **2027** and always tries to squeeze the price.
do: Keep the **same hens and staff** on Coldharbour Farm.
Build a separate **£20,000 reserve** for a bird flu year.
Use AI **now and then** for letters to the packer.
feel: A little uneasy, with **the old unease** that wears feathers.
S0.quote: One case of bird flu at Coldharbour Farm could cost me more than any computer ever will.
fieldNote: His pre-existing pressures, **bird flu and contracts**, keep him uneasy even with no AI change.
He adopted AI only after **Hugh's demonstration**, a classic steady adopter.
Owning the farm with good equity gives him **real security** beneath the worry.

steps.text: Keep the same 16,000 hens and staff
Build a separate £20,000 reserve for a bird flu year

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's progress, as long as people still have to work for their living. At the farm meeting I'd say let's see who gets good results first. I wouldn't be the first to say it's wonderful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it would help us a bit. The packer would use AI for orders and grading, and Abena could do the books faster. But the packer's office staff would go, and the ones left would be even harder to negotiate with.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait one season and see what Hugh and the others try. Then I'd ask Abena to use an accounts program that does more of the work. Stan and Jola carry on, because a robot can't collect eggs from 16,000 hens yet, not in this picture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but steady. The birds don't care, and the bird flu worry stays the same.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who in your world would feel this picture most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Abena, oddly, because her work is the books and the sales. My wife Abena could do the farm accounts in half the time, and I worry what the other half of her day becomes. She'd find something, she always does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait a season. Why not jump in?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the first one through the gate gets kicked. My father taught me that with cattle and it's true of machines. Let Hugh find the problems.

say: I'd call it **progress**, if people still work for their living.
I'd say at the farm meeting, see **who gets results** first.
think: It would **help us a bit**: Abena does the books faster.
The packer's leaner office would be **harder to negotiate** with.
do: Wait **one season** and watch what Hugh tries.
Ask Abena to use an **accounts program** that does more of the work.
Keep **Stan and Jola** on the egg collecting.
feel: Uneasy but **steady**, with the bird flu worry unchanged.
S1.quote: My wife Abena could do the farm accounts in half the time, and I worry what the other half of her day becomes.
fieldNote: He spots a subtle risk: a **leaner packer** with more bargaining power.
His worry for **Abena's role** is gentle and concrete.
His waiting rule comes from his **father's cattle saying**.

steps.text: Wait one season and watch Hugh's results
Move Abena onto an AI accounts program
Keep Stan and Jola collecting and packing eggs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is too fast and the government should keep its hands off and let farmers adapt. At church I'd say we look after our own, our workers and our families. I wouldn't march about it, that's not me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I'd worry. By 2031 the big egg firms would have robot sheds running night and day, and my eggs would cost more than theirs. The farm is still ours, but the income could shrink fast if the packer finds cheaper eggs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd hold off any spending on the sheds and keep the cash, because I wouldn't know which way to jump. Once Hugh or someone proves a robot egg collector, I'd buy one, maybe 2031 or 2032. And I'd talk to Stan and Jola honestly, early, so they have time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, properly worried. But I'd still sleep, mostly. We have the farm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thinking AI comes in 2028 and robots about 3 years later. How does that gap play out on Coldharbour?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2028 the packer and the supermarkets get cleverer at squeezing, and Abena's books are done by a program. The hens still need hands until 2031. Those three years are when I'd decide whether to compete with robots or rent the sheds to someone who has them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Stan and Jola?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The truth, and soon. Stan has collected eggs at Coldharbour Farm for nine years, and I'd owe Stan the truth before any robot salesman visits. I'd give them good references and a proper payout.

say: I'd say government should **let farmers adapt**, not take over.
I'd say at church we **look after our own**.
think: Big egg firms with **robot sheds** would undercut me by 2031.
The farm is ours, but **income could shrink** fast.
do: Freeze **shed spending** and keep cash until the way is clear.
Buy a **robot egg collector** once someone proves it, around 2031.
Tell **Stan and Jola** honestly and early, with a proper payout.
S2.quote: Stan has collected eggs at Coldharbour Farm for nine years, and I'd owe Stan the truth before any robot salesman visits.
fieldNote: His risk is **price competition**, not losing the land.
Traditional duty shows in his care for **Stan and Jola**.
He wants government to **stay out**, not to step in.

steps.text: Freeze spending on the hen sheds and keep cash
Buy a robot egg collector once a neighbour proves one
Wait to see how the packer's prices move after 2028

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is fair warning for a sensible man. At the farm meeting I'd say watch, learn, and don't borrow too much. At church I'd say it's in God's hands, and in ours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd be all right. Five years lets me see which robots work, and I'd have the egg contract renewed in 2027. The worry is the price, not the farm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd renew the egg contract for five years if the packer will do it. Around 2030 I'd buy a robot egg collector for one shed, once Hugh has tested his. I'd put Kwame's name down for an agricultural engineering apprenticeship when he's sixteen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, the ordinary kind. I can plan for this one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Your work is mostly hands-on. What changes for you in 2031, before the robots?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Abena's work changes most, and the dealing with the packer. I'd use the AI to check the packer's prices against the market, which I can't do properly now. A computer that shows me what the egg packer pays everyone else would be worth more to me than any robot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why an apprenticeship for Kwame, not university?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because a lad learns best beside someone who knows the job. And whoever fixes the robots will never be short of work. If he wants university after, good.

I'd tell the farm meeting to **watch, learn** and not borrow too much.
think: I'd be **all right**: time to see which robots work.
The worry is **the egg price**, not the farm itself.
do: Renew the **egg contract** for five years if possible.
Buy a **robot egg collector** for one shed around 2030.
Put Kwame down for an **engineering apprenticeship** at sixteen.
feel: Uneasy, **the ordinary kind**, because he can plan.
S3.quote: A computer that shows me what the egg packer pays everyone else would be worth more to me than any robot.
fieldNote: Five years matches his **steady, proven-first** style.
He'd use AI as a **bargaining tool** against the packer.
He prefers an **apprenticeship** over university for Kwame, learning beside someone who knows the job.

steps.text: Renew the egg contract with the packer for five years
Buy a robot egg collector for one shed around 2030
Sign Kwame up for an agricultural engineering apprenticeship

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, and people should stop complaining and start preparing. I'd say the farm will still be here, run differently. I'd keep politics out of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be uneasy only about the old worries. I'd be fifty-six in 2039, with the farm loan mostly paid and the robots proven by others. Bird flu would still be my biggest fear, robot or no robot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going much as I do now for five or six years. Around 2035 I'd build a new robot-ready shed with the savings and a small loan, maybe 8,000 more birds. And I'd help Stan move into minding the robots if he's willing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, a little. Mostly I'd feel ready.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Kwame and Grace?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That hard work and a skill will see them right, whatever the machines do. I'd tell my son Kwame that the man who can mend the robot will always eat before the man who bought it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said bird flu stays your biggest fear. Even with AGI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Even then. Robots can't stop wild birds flying over the sheds. A clever machine might spot it sooner, I'll give it that.

I'd say the farm will **still be here**, run differently.
think: I'd be fifty-six in 2039 with **the loan mostly paid**.
**Bird flu** would still be my biggest fear, robot or no robot.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because the big egg firms would get their robots before I'd seen any proven. What would help is fair rules so the packers can't squeeze small farms out, and apprenticeships so young people learn the new trades. I don't want money from the government, I want a fair market.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask about the land itself. Machines come and go, but somebody has to care for the soil. I bought Coldharbour Farm with a mortgage and a prayer, and no machine will love those fields the way I do.

headlineQuote: I bought Coldharbour Farm with a mortgage and a prayer, and no machine will love those fields the way I do.

Fast AGI makes him anxious about **robot-run egg firms** undercutting him.
He wants a **fair market** and apprenticeships, not government money.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, with big egg firms getting proven robots before him.
